mcqs.q: In the program that prints each digit on a separate line, the first while loop finds:
options: The divisor of the largest place
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the divisor of the largest place. The lesson explains that the first loop finds this divisor, and the second loop then prints each digit from left to right on a separate line.

mcqs.q: In the square-box program made with nested loops, the outer loop runs the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: rows. The lesson explains that in the box program the outer loop runs the rows and the inner loop prints the character in each row.

mcqs.q: A prime number, as used in the lesson's program, is a number that is divided only by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 1 and itself. The lesson defines a prime number this way, and its program checks n % i == 0 for i from 2 to n / 2 to detect a non-prime.

mcqs.q: In the star-pattern program (one star, then two, then three per row), the inner loop runs j from 1 to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: i, the current row number. The lesson's pattern program uses for (j = 1; j <= i; j++) inside the outer loop, so each row prints as many stars as its row number.

mcqs.q: In the program printing squares of numbers from 1 to 10, the line printed for 7 is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: '7 square = 49'. The lesson lists the program's output as 1 square = 1, 2 square = 4, and so on up to 10 square = 100, so 7 gives 49.

lessons.notes_html:
Program: odd or even

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int num; cout << "Enter a number"; cin >> num; if (num % 2 == 0) cout << "Even"; else cout << "Odd"; return 0; }

If dividing the number by 2 leaves remainder 0, it is even, otherwise odd.

Program: add numbers from 1 to 20

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int i, sum = 0; for (i = 1; i <= 20; i++) sum = sum + i; cout << "Sum = " << sum; return 0; }

Output: Sum = 210.

Program: number of days in a month (switch)

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int month; cout << "Enter month number 1 to 12"; cin >> month; switch (month) { case 1: case 3: case 5: case 7: case 8: case 10: case 12: cout << "31 days"; break; case 4: case 6: case 9: case 11: cout << "30 days"; break; case 2: cout << "28 days"; break; default: cout << "Wrong number / Error message"; } return 0; }

February is written as 28 days; the book does not give the leap-year case.

Program: each digit on a separate line

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int num, divisor = 1, temp; cout << "Enter a number up to six digits"; cin >> num; temp = num; while (temp >= 10) { divisor = divisor * 10; temp = temp / 10; } while (divisor > 0) { cout << num / divisor << endl; num = num % divisor; divisor = divisor / 10; } return 0; }

The first loop finds the divisor of the largest place, the second loop prints each digit from left to right on a separate line.

Program: square box filled with a character (nested loops)

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { char ch; int rows, cols, i, j; cout << "Enter character, rows and columns"; cin >> ch >> rows >> cols; for (i = 1; i <= rows; i++) { for (j = 1; j <= cols; j++) cout << ch; cout << endl; } return 0; }

The outer loop runs the rows, the inner loop prints the character in each row.

Programs: number patterns with nested loops

(1) Stars (* / ** / *** / **** / *****): for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { for (j = 1; j <= i; j++) cout << "*"; cout << endl; }

(2) Numbers (1 / 12 / 123 / 1234 / 12345): for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { for (j = 1; j <= i; j++) cout << j; cout << endl; }

(3) Same number (1 / 22 / 333 / 4444 / 55555): for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { for (j = 1; j <= i; j++) cout << i; cout << endl; }

All three are made with nested loops — the outer loop runs the row, the inner loop runs the items of each row.

Program: prime or not

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int n, i; bool isPrime = true; cout << "Enter a number"; cin >> n; if (n <= 1) isPrime = false; for (i = 2; i <= n / 2; i++) { if (n % i == 0) isPrime = false; } if (isPrime) cout << "Prime"; else cout << "Not Prime"; return 0; }

A prime number is one that is divided only by 1 and itself.

Program: designation from salary (else if ladder)

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { float salary; cout << "Enter salary"; cin >> salary; if (salary >= 100000) cout << "Manager"; else if (salary >= 50000) cout << "Supervisor"; else cout << "Worker"; return 0; }

The book does not fix salary limits; the limits above are given as an example.

Program: squares of numbers from 1 to 10

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int i; for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++) cout << i << " square = " << i * i << endl; return 0; }

Output: 1 square = 1, 2 square = 4, 3 square = 9, 4 square = 16, 5 square = 25, 6 square = 36, 7 square = 49, 8 square = 64, 9 square = 81, 10 square = 100.

Program: table of a number using while loop

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int n, i = 1; cout << "Enter a number"; cin >> n; while (i <= 10) { cout << n << " x " << i << " = " << n * i << endl; i++; } return 0; }

For example, for 2 the output is: 2 x 1 = 2, 2 x 2 = 4, 2 x 3 = 6, ..., 2 x 10 = 20.

lessons.title: Functions: Built-in and User-defined; Declaration and Definition

mcqs.q: User-defined functions are the functions that are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: defined by the programmer. The lesson says the programmer can write their own functions to perform a specific task, and these are called user-defined functions.

mcqs.q: Built-in or predefined functions are the functions that are:
options: Written by the user for each program
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: already given by C++. The lesson contrasts built-in (predefined) functions with user-defined ones, and notes that predefined functions are declared in header files.

mcqs.q: The word 'prototype' in functions means:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: declaration. The lesson states directly that the word 'prototype' means declaration, and a function declaration tells the compiler about the function's name, return data type and argument data types.

mcqs.q: A function prototype or declaration tells the compiler about:
options: The function's name, return data type and arguments or parameter data types
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the function's name, return data type and arguments or parameter data types. The lesson gives this full description of a function declaration, which ends with a semicolon.

mcqs.q: A function declaration differs from a definition because the declaration:
options: Is a function without its definition (code block) and is declared before main()
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: it is a function without its definition (code block) and is declared before main(). The lesson's comparison table gives this difference, while the definition itself has a header and a body.

mcqs.q: A function definition consists of:
options: A header and a body or code block with statements in braces
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: a header and a body or code block. The lesson says the header has the return value data type, the function name and the list of arguments in parenthesis, and the body has statements in braces.

mcqs.q: The void keyword is used in a function when:
options: No value is returned by the function
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: when no value is returned by the function. The lesson also notes that void is used when there is no parameter, for example void function name(void);

mcqs.q: Header files, through which predefined functions are included in a program, have the extension:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: .h. The lesson says a header file has the .h extension, predefined functions are declared in header files, and they are included in the program with #include.

mcqs.q: In C++, int main() returns a value of which data type, by default, to the operating system?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: int, an integer value. The lesson states that in C++, int main() returns an int (integer) data type value by default to the operating system.

mcqs.q: A function declaration ends with:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: a semicolon (;). The lesson's declaration-versus-definition table states that a declaration ends with a semicolon, unlike the definition which carries the body.

lessons.notes_html:
Two kinds of functions

The functions that are defined by the programmer are called user-defined functions — the programmer can write their own functions to perform a specific task. The functions already given by C++ are the built-in (predefined) functions.

Function prototype (declaration)

The word "prototype" means declaration. The function prototype consists of all of these: the name of the function, the parameters passed to the function, and the value returned from the function — a function declaration tells the compiler about the function's name, return data type and arguments/parameter data types.

Function declaration vs function definition

DeclarationDefinition
A function without its definition (code block); declared before main()The function itself; it has a header and a body / code block
Tells the compiler about the function's name, return data type, and arguments/parameter data types; ends with a semicolon (;)The header has the return value data type, the function name and the list of arguments with datatypes in parenthesis; the body has statements in braces; the definition may be before or after the main function

The void keyword

void is used when no value is returned by the function. If there is no parameter in the function, void is also used, for example void function name(void);

Including a function through a header file

A programmer creates a function for a particular task and includes that function in the program through a header file, which has the .h extension — predefined functions are declared in header files and included in the program with #include.

main() returns int

In C++, int main() returns an int (integer) data type value by default to the operating system.

lessons.title: Header Files, Built-in Functions and Variable Scope

mcqs.q: To use the sqrt() function, which header file is included?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: cmath. The lesson gives header file examples: cmath for sqrt(), cstdio for gets() and puts(), and conio.h for getch() and getche().

mcqs.q: The getch() function belongs to which header file?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: conio.h. The lesson lists getch() among the built-in functions and states that conio.h is the header file for getch() and getche().

mcqs.q: The built-in function sqrt(a) finds:
options: The square root of a number
The upper case of a character
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the square root of a number. The lesson lists sqrt(a) first among the five standard built-in functions with this meaning.

mcqs.q: The built-in function pow(x, y) finds:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: x to the power y. The lesson describes pow(x, y) as finding x to the power y in its list of standard built-in functions.

mcqs.q: The built-in function strcpy(str1, str2) is used to:
options: Copy one string into another string
Convert a character to upper case
Read a character from the keyboard
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: copy one string into another string. The lesson gives this meaning for strcpy(str1, str2) among the five standard built-in functions.

mcqs.q: The built-in function toupper(ch) converts:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: a character to upper case. The lesson lists toupper(ch) with exactly this meaning among the standard built-in functions.

mcqs.q: The parameters specified in the function header are called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: formal parameters. The lesson states that the parameters specified in the function header are called formal parameters.

mcqs.q: Local variables are the variables that are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: declared inside any function. The lesson says all variables declared in a function definition are called local variables, and they are accessible only within that specific part of the program.

mcqs.q: External or global variables are declared:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: outside of the main function. The lesson adds that global variables hold their value during the entire execution of the program and their value can be shared with different functions.

mcqs.q: One advantage of user-defined functions is that:
options: They make programs impossible to manage
Large and complicated programs are broken down into smaller modules or functions
They can be called only once
They remove the need for main()
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: large and complicated programs are broken down into smaller modules or functions. The lesson also says functions help manage the code of a large program and a function written once can be called from any part of the program.

lessons.notes_html:
Why we use header files

Predefined functions are declared in header files; to use them the proper header file is included with #include, for example cmath for sqrt(), cstdio for gets() / puts(), conio.h for getch() / getche(). Header files link the external header files / libraries which may be required in the program.

Five standard built-in functions

  • sqrt(a): finds the square root of a number.
  • pow(x, y): finds x to the power y.
  • strcpy(str1, str2): copies one string into another string.
  • toupper(ch): converts a character to upper case.
  • getch(): gets a single character from the keyboard.

Parameters: formal and actual

The parameters specified in the function header are called formal parameters. All variables declared in a function definition are called local variables.

Local variables vs external (global) variables

External / global variablesLocal variables
Declared outside of the main function; also known as external variablesDeclared inside any function (also in the header of the function definition)
Hold the value of the variable during the entire execution of the program; their value can be shared with different functionsOnly accessible within a specific part of the program / that function

Advantages of user-defined functions

  • Large and complicated programs are broken down into smaller modules / functions.
  • Functions help the programmer to manage the code of the large program.
  • A function written once can be called from any part of the program.
  • The programmer can create functions for a specific task.

lessons.title: Passing Arguments and Returning Values

mcqs.q: When a function is called, the values given with the function call are:
options: Actual values, which can be variables or constants
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: actual values, which can be variables or constants. The lesson says that when the function is called, actual values are given with the call and received in the formal parameters.

mcqs.q: The actual values given in a function call are received in:
options: The formal parameters of the function definition
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the formal parameters of the function definition. The lesson adds that these formal parameters act as local variables inside the function.

mcqs.q: Inside a function, its formal parameters act as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: local variables. The lesson states that the formal parameters of the function definition act as local variables inside the function.

mcqs.q: When a function completes its execution, the return keyword sends back to the calling function:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: a single value. The lesson says the return keyword sends a single value back to the calling function when the function completes its execution.

mcqs.q: The return data type of a function must be specified:
options: In the header, before the function name
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: in the header, before the function name. The lesson adds that the return data type must be specified in both the function declaration and the definition.

mcqs.q: In the lesson's error-finding program, the error in the prototype line was that \\ was written, but in C++ a comment needs:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: //. The lesson explains that \\ is not a comment in C++; a comment needs //, so the corrected line is: void Table(void); // Function prototype.

mcqs.q: The corrected prototype line in that program is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: void Table(void); // Function prototype. The lesson says there is no other error in that program once the comment is written with // instead of \\

mcqs.q: For input m = 5, the program first prints:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 'The value of m....... 5'. The lesson gives this as the first line of the output for input m = 5, followed by the table of 5.

mcqs.q: In the table of 5 printed by that program, the line for 7 is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 5*7=35. The lesson lists the table output as 5*1=5, 5*2=10, and so on up to 5*10=50, so the line for 7 is 5*7=35.

mcqs.q: The return data type must be specified in:
options: Both the function declaration and the definition
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: both the function declaration and the definition. The lesson states this requirement clearly in its section on returning a value from a function.

lessons.notes_html:
Passing an argument to a function

When the function is called, actual values (variables or constants) are given with the function call; they are received in the formal parameters of the function definition, which act as local variables inside the function.

Returning a value from a function

When the function completes its execution, the return keyword sends a single value back to the calling function; the return data type must be specified in the header, before the function name, in both the function declaration and the definition.

Finding the error and the output of a program

Error: in the function prototype line, \\ is written, which is not a comment in C++; a comment needs //: void Table(void); // Function prototype. There is no other error. Output (for input m = 5): The value of m....... 5; then the table of 5: 5*1=5, 5*2=10, 5*3=15, 5*4=20, 5*5=25, 5*6=30, 5*7=35, 5*8=40, 5*9=45, 5*10=50.

lessons.title: Programs Using Functions

mcqs.q: The series() function in the lesson's program is declared as void series(void), which means it:
options: Returns an integer and takes one parameter
Neither returns a value nor takes parameters
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: it neither returns a value nor takes parameters. The lesson points to the form void function name(void) for such a function, and series() is called from main() with no arguments.

mcqs.q: The series() function prints numbers starting from 0, increasing by 5 each time, up to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 35. The lesson's output of the series program is 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 35, because the loop runs i from 0 while i <= 35 with i = i + 5.

mcqs.q: In the even-or-odd function program, checkEven(num) returns 1 when:
options: n % 2 == 0, that is, the number is even
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: when n % 2 == 0, that is, the number is even. The lesson's checkEven function returns 1 in this case and 0 otherwise, and main() prints 'Even' when the result is 1.

mcqs.q: The kgToGrams function converts kilograms into grams by returning:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: kg x 1000. The lesson's function takes the value in kilograms as a parameter and returns kg * 1000 as the value in grams.

mcqs.q: In the star box program, starBox(10, 4) returns a total of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 40 stars. The lesson's program prints 4 rows of 10 stars and then 'Total stars = 40', because the function returns length x height.

mcqs.q: The starBox function returns its total by computing:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: length x height. After printing the box with nested loops, the lesson's starBox function returns length * height as the total number of stars.

mcqs.q: In the factorial function, the factorial is calculated as:
options: f starts at 1 and is multiplied by each i from 1 to n
f starts at 0 and adds n
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: f starts at 1 and is multiplied by each i from 1 to n. The lesson's factorial function uses a loop f = f * i, matching the meaning n! = 1 x 2 x ... x n.

mcqs.q: The rectArea function in the lesson returns the area of a rectangle as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: l x w. The lesson gives the formula function float rectArea(float l, float w) { return l * w; } for the area of a rectangle.

mcqs.q: The circleArea function uses pi = 3.14 and returns:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 3.14 x r x r. The lesson gives float circleArea(float r) { return 3.14 * r * r; } for the area of a circle.

mcqs.q: The hypotenuse function, from c2 = a2 + b2, returns:
options: sqrt(a x a + b x b)
a x a + b x b without the square root
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: sqrt(a * a + b * b). The lesson derives c = sqrt(a2 + b2) from the Pythagorean theorem and gives the function returning exactly this.

lessons.notes_html:
Series program — no return value and no parameters

#include<iostream> using namespace std; void series(void); int main() { series(); return 0; } void series(void) { int i; for (i = 0; i <= 35; i = i + 5) cout << i << " "; }

Output: 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 35. The function neither returns a value nor takes parameters: void function name(void);

Even or odd — return value and pass parameters

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int checkEven(int n); int main() { int num, result; cout << "Enter a number"; cin >> num; result = checkEven(num); if (result == 1) cout << "Even"; else cout << "Odd"; return 0; } int checkEven(int n) { if (n % 2 == 0) return 1; else return 0; }

The function takes a parameter and returns a value: int function name(int);

Convert kilograms into grams using a function

#include<iostream> using namespace std; float kgToGrams(float kg); int main() { float kg, grams; cout << "Enter kilograms"; cin >> kg; grams = kgToGrams(kg); cout << "Grams = " << grams; return 0; } float kgToGrams(float kg) { return kg * 1000; }

The function takes the value in kilograms as a parameter and returns the value in grams.

Box of stars function

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int starBox(int length, int height); int main() { int total; total = starBox(10, 4); cout << "Total stars = " << total; return 0; } int starBox(int length, int height) { int i, j; for (i = 1; i <= height; i++) { for (j = 1; j <= length; j++) cout << "*"; cout << endl; } return length * height; }

Output: 4 rows of 10 stars, then Total stars = 40.

Factorial function

#include<iostream> using namespace std; int factorial(int n); int main() { int num; cout << "Enter a number"; cin >> num; cout << "Factorial = " << factorial(num); return 0; } int factorial(int n) { int i, f = 1; for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) f = f * i; return f; }

Factorial means n! = 1 x 2 x ... x n.

Formula functions

  • Area of rectangle a = l x w: float rectArea(float l, float w) { return l * w; }
  • Area of circle a = pi r2 (pi = 3.14): float circleArea(float r) { return 3.14 * r * r; }
  • Pythagorean theorem c2 = a2 + b2: float hypotenuse(float a, float b) { return sqrt(a * a + b * b); } — from c2 = a2 + b2, c = sqrt(a2 + b2).

Each function is called from main() with parameters and returns the result.

lessons.title: Basic Logic Gates: AND, OR and NOT

mcqs.q: The AND gate has:
options: Two or more inputs and a single output
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: two or more inputs and a single output. The lesson states this for both the AND gate and the OR gate, while the NOT gate has a single input and a single output.

mcqs.q: The AND gate operates on logical multiplication, with the expression:
options: Y = A with a bar over it
Y = (A.B) with a bar over it
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Y = A.B. The lesson says the AND gate operates on logical multiplication, while the OR gate operates on logical addition with Y = A + B.

mcqs.q: The output of an AND gate is 1 only when:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: when all inputs are 1. The AND truth table in the lesson shows Y = 1 only for A = 1 and B = 1, and if any input is 0 the output is 0.

mcqs.q: For an AND gate, if any input is 0, the output is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 0. The lesson states this rule for the AND gate, whose truth table shows output 0 for the combinations 0,0 and 0,1 and 1,0.

mcqs.q: The OR gate operates on logical addition, with the expression:
options: Y = (A + B) with a bar over it
Y = A with a bar over it
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Y = A + B. The lesson says the OR gate operates on logical addition, in contrast to the AND gate's logical multiplication.

mcqs.q: The output of an OR gate is 1 when:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: when any input is 1. The OR truth table in the lesson shows output 1 for 0,1 and 1,0 and 1,1, and output 0 only if all inputs are 0.

mcqs.q: The NOT gate is also called the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: inverter. The lesson says the NOT gate has a single input and a single output, is the inverter, and has the expression Y = A with a bar over it.

mcqs.q: In the NOT gate expression Y = A with a bar over A, the bar sign indicates:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the NOT operation. The lesson states that the bar sign over a variable indicates the NOT operation, so the gate inverts its input.

mcqs.q: If the input of a NOT gate is 1, its output is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 0. The lesson's NOT truth table shows that the inverter inverts the input: if the input is 1 the output is 0, and if the input is 0 the output is 1.

mcqs.q: Which gate has a single input and a single output?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the NOT gate. The lesson describes the NOT gate with a single input and a single output, while the AND and OR gates have two or more inputs and a single output.

The AND gate has two or more inputs and a single output; it operates on logical multiplication; Y = A.B; the output is 1 only when all inputs are 1 — if any input is 0 the output is 0.

lessons.title: Universal Gates: NAND and NOR

mcqs.q: The universal gates are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the NAND gate and the NOR gate. The lesson states directly that the NAND gate and the NOR gate are the universal gates.

mcqs.q: The NAND gate is the collection of:
options: An OR gate and a NOT gate in series
An AND gate and a NOT gate connected in series
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: an AND gate and a NOT gate connected in series. The lesson also calls the NAND gate NOT-AND for this reason.

mcqs.q: The Boolean expression of the NAND gate is:
options: Y = (A.B) with a bar over the whole expression
Y = A with a bar over it
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Y = (A.B) with a bar over the whole expression. The lesson explains that when A and B go into an AND gate and its output passes through a NOT gate, the circuit is a NAND gate with this expression.

mcqs.q: The output of a NAND gate is 0 only when:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: when all inputs are 1. The lesson states this for the NAND gate, and adds that if any one of the inputs is 0 the output is 1.

mcqs.q: For a NAND gate, if any one of the inputs is 0, the output is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 1. This follows from the lesson's NAND rule: the output is 0 only when all inputs are 1, so any 0 input makes the output 1.

mcqs.q: The NOR gate is the collection of:
options: An AND gate and a NOT gate
An OR gate and a NOT gate, giving an inverted OR
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: an OR gate and a NOT gate, and its output is inverted OR. The lesson gives the NOR expression as Y = (A + B) with a bar over the whole expression.

mcqs.q: The output of a NOR gate is 1 only when:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: when both inputs are 0. The lesson states this for the NOR gate, and adds that if any one of the inputs is 1 the output is 0.

mcqs.q: For a NOR gate, if any one of the inputs is 1, the output is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 0. This is the lesson's NOR rule: its output is 1 only when both inputs are 0, so a single 1 input forces the output to 0.

mcqs.q: Which gate's expression is Y = (A + B) with a bar over the whole expression?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the NOR gate. The lesson's NAND-versus-NOR table gives (A + B) with a bar for NOR and (A.B) with a bar for NAND.

mcqs.q: A circuit in which A and B pass through an AND gate and then through a NOT gate is a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: a NAND gate. The lesson uses exactly this circuit to explain the NAND gate, whose Boolean expression is (A.B) with a bar over it.

lessons.notes_html:
Universal gates

The NAND gate and the NOR gate are the universal gates.

The NAND gate

NAND gate (NOT-AND) is the collection of an AND gate and a NOT gate connected in series; Y = (A.B) with a bar over it; the output is 0 only when all inputs are 1 — if any one of the inputs is 0 the output is 1. So, when A and B go into an AND gate and its output passes through a NOT gate, the Boolean expression of the circuit is (A.B) with a bar over it — the circuit is a NAND gate.

The NOR gate

The NOR gate is the collection of an OR gate and a NOT gate; its output is inverted OR; Y = (A+B) with a bar over it; the output is 1 only when both inputs are 0 — if any one of the inputs is 1 the output is 0.

lessons.title: Boolean Algebra and Truth Tables

mcqs.q: Boolean algebra is used to:
options: Describe the logical operations and processing of binary information
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: describe the logical operations and processing of binary information. The lesson adds that its pre-defined rules help to simplify the logical expression.

mcqs.q: Simplifying a logical expression with Boolean algebra rules helps to:
options: Reduce the number of logic gates needed for a logic operation
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: reduce the number of logic gates needed to perform a particular logic operation. The lesson gives this as the purpose of simplifying expressions with the rules of Boolean algebra.

mcqs.q: A truth table is:
options: A tabular representation of all combinations of values for inputs and their corresponding outputs
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: a tabular representation of all the combinations of values for inputs and their corresponding outputs. The lesson defines a truth table in exactly these words.

mcqs.q: With three variables, a truth table has how many combinations or rows?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: eight, from 2 x 2 x 2. The lesson states that with the combination of three variables, eight outputs are expected altogether.

mcqs.q: Rule 2 of Boolean algebra states:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 1 + A = 1. The lesson's rule list gives this as Rule 2, while A . 1 = A is Rule 4 and A + A = A is Rule 5.

mcqs.q: Rule 4 of Boolean algebra states:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: A . 1 = A. The lesson's list of Boolean algebra rules gives A . 1 = A as Rule 4. Multiplying any Boolean value by 1 leaves it unchanged, so the result is the value itself.

mcqs.q: A + A = A is which rule of Boolean algebra?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Rule 5. The lesson states plainly that A + A = A is the 5th rule of Boolean algebra, in its list of rules used in this unit.

mcqs.q: Rule 7 of Boolean algebra, A . A = A, gives for example:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: B . B = B. The lesson gives this example for Rule 7, A . A = A, in its list of Boolean algebra rules.

mcqs.q: A . A-bar = 0 is which rule of Boolean algebra?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Rule 8. The lesson states that A . A-bar = 0 is the 8th rule of Boolean algebra. A variable combined with its own complement always gives 0, because the two can never be 1 at the same time.

mcqs.q: Rule 11 of Boolean algebra, A-bar + A.B = A-bar + B, gives for example:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: B-bar + B.C = B-bar + C. The lesson gives exactly this example for Rule 11 in its list of Boolean algebra rules used in this unit.

lessons.notes_html:
Why we use Boolean algebra

Boolean algebra is used to describe the logical operations and processing of binary information; its pre-defined rules help to simplify the logical expression, so that the number of logic gates needed to perform a particular logic operation is reduced.

Truth tables

A truth table is a tabular representation of all the combinations of values for inputs and their corresponding outputs. With the combination of three variables, eight outputs are expected altogether — for three variables the truth table has 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations / rows.

So A+A=A is the 5th rule of Boolean algebra, and A.Ā=0 is the 8th rule.

lessons.title: Simplifying Expressions and Designing Circuits

mcqs.q: In simplifying expressions, B.B simplifies to B by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Rule 7, because A . A = A. The lesson uses this step when expanding Z = AB + A(B + C) + B(B + C), where BB becomes B by Rule 7.

mcqs.q: AB + AB simplifies to AB by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Rule 5, because A + A = A. The lesson notes this step in the same simplification, where the repeated AB term is written once.

mcqs.q: B + BC simplifies to B by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Rule 10, because A + A.B = A. The lesson applies this rule to reduce B + BC to B while simplifying the expression for Z.

mcqs.q: The expression Z = AB + A(B + C) + B(B + C) simplifies finally to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Z = B + AC. The lesson expands the expression, reduces B + BC to B, and then uses Rule 2 and Rule 4 to reach the final simplified form Z = B + AC.

mcqs.q: In that simplification, the step B(1 + A) + AC becomes B + AC because:
options: 1 + A = 1 by Rule 2, and B . 1 = B by Rule 4
A-bar + A.B = A-bar + B by Rule 11
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: 1 + A = 1 by Rule 2, and B . 1 = B by Rule 4. The lesson names both rules at this final step of simplifying Z.

mcqs.q: The expression ABC + AB C-bar + A-bar B simplifies to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: B. The lesson takes AB common from the first two parts to get AB(C + C-bar) = AB, and then AB + A-bar B = B(A + A-bar) = B.

mcqs.q: The expression ABC + A-bar BC simplifies to:
options: BC, by taking BC common: BC(A + A-bar) = BC
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: BC. The lesson takes BC common from both parts, giving BC(A + A-bar) = BC(1) = BC as the simplified form.

mcqs.q: In the logic circuit of the 10th law, A + A.B = A, the circuit first sends A and B into:
options: An OR gate to give A + B
An AND gate to give A.B
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: an AND gate to give A.B. The lesson then sends A and A.B into an OR gate to give A + A.B, whose output is A.

mcqs.q: In the expression Q with two A.B parts and a bar over (A + B), Q simplifies to AB + (A + B)-bar because:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: AB + AB = AB by Rule 5. The lesson notes that A.B is printed twice in the expression, and Rule 5 combines the two identical parts into one.

mcqs.q: The circuit expression Y = ABC + A(B-bar + C-bar) simplifies finally to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: Y = A. The lesson simplifies step by step using Rule 11 and then Rules 6, 2 and 4, ending with the simplified form Y = A.

lessons.notes_html:
Simplify: Z = AB + A(B + C) + B(B + C)

Expand: AB + AB + AC + BB + BC = AB + AC + B + BC (because BB = B, Rule 7, and AB + AB = AB, Rule 5). B + BC = B (Rule 10: A + A.B = A). Then Z = AB + AC + B = B + AB + AC = B(1 + A) + AC = B + AC (Rule 2: 1 + A = 1; Rule 4: B.1 = B). So Z = B + AC.

Simplify: two short expressions

  • ABC + ABĈ + ĀB = B — take AB common from the first two parts: AB(C + Ĉ) = AB(1) = AB; then AB + ĀB = B(A + Ā) = B(1) = B.
  • ABC + ĀBC = BC — take BC common: BC(A + Ā) = BC(1) = BC.

Logic circuit of the 10th law of Boolean algebra

10th Rule: A + A.B = A. Circuit: A and B go into an AND gate to give A.B; then A and A.B go into an OR gate to give A + A.B, whose output is A.

Designing a circuit from a Boolean expression

Expression: Q = (A.B) + (A.B) + (A+B) with a bar over (A+B). Circuit: two AND gates (both with A and B) give the two A.B parts; one OR gate (with A and B) followed by a NOT gate gives (A+B) with a bar over it; then the three parts go into a three-input OR gate, whose output is Q. Note: A.B is printed twice in the expression; AB + AB = AB (Rule 5), so Q = AB + (A+B) with a bar over (A+B).

From a circuit to the expression, truth table and simplification

Circuit: A, B, C into a three-input AND gate; B and C through NOT gates into an OR gate; A and (B̄ + C̄) into an AND gate; both results into a final OR gate. Expression: Y = ABC + A(B̄ + C̄).

mcqs.why: The correct answer is: remember codes. The lesson gives this as a feature of Scratch, because programs are made by joining blocks instead of typing memorized code.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the Cat. The lesson states that Cat is the default sprite, and that at least one sprite is always needed in a project.

The set of step-wise instructions given to the sprite to do a particular task

options: The same backdrop as the stage

options: The background added on the stage
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: the background added on the stage. The lesson adds that the look of the stage can be changed by adding new backdrops.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is: no backdrop is added. The lesson states this directly, and says the look of the stage can be changed by adding new backdrops.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is: one sprite and code. The lesson says a Scratch program is at least made up of one sprite and code, at least one sprite is always needed, and multiple sprites are possible.

lessons.notes_html:
Features of Scratch

  • It is a visual language.
  • It is free forever.
  • There is no need to remember codes.

All of these are features of Scratch.

Sprite, script and backdrop

  • Script: the set of step-wise instructions given to the sprite to do a particular task; scripts are instructions that make sprites perform a task; each sprite has its own script area.
  • Sprite: the images of cartoons, characters or objects added in the project — the character which moves on the Stage is called a sprite. We can have multiple sprites in a project but at least one sprite is always needed; Cat is the default sprite.
  • Backdrop: the background added on the stage; by default, no backdrop is added in a project; the look of the stage can be changed by adding new backdrops.

What a Scratch program is made of

A Scratch program is at least made up of one sprite and code — at least one sprite is always needed for the project, and every sprite has its own code / script.

Coordinates on the stage

To change the position of a sprite on the screen, we use coordinates — the stage is divided into x (horizontal) and y (vertical) coordinates; the go to x, y command changes the position of the sprite.
